This field study at Logan, Utah compares pollination efficiency of native bees versus honey bees on sunflower, finding Melissodes agilis (both sexes) to be the most effective and most faithful pollinator across all sterile/fertile line combinations, producing far more seeds per visit than Apis mellifera and carrying substantially more pollen (up to ~104,500 grains per female) than any other bee group studied.

This paper gives one of the few available nest descriptions for the genus Melissodes, documenting a complete nest of Melissodes floris (subgenus Eumelissodes) found within a dense multi-species bee aggregation on a roadside bank near San Miguel Duenas, Guatemala. It reports burrow and cell dimensions, provision character, and notes that three dead M. floris females each carried a puparium of a phorid fly (Phoridae) in the thorax, indicating parasitism of the bee by this fly.

This paper reports the pollen foraging preferences of Melissodes (Ecplectica) tintinnans and M. (Ecplectica) rufithorax in a commercial sunflower field and its field margins near Carlos Casares, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina, based on scopal and body-hair pollen load analysis over a full growing season. It shows both species rely heavily on Helianthus annuus pollen during bloom but shift to Bidens sp. and Baccharis sp. after bloom, classifying M. tintinnans as eclectic oligolectic and M. rufithorax as broadly oligolectic on Asteraceae, and highlights the role of hedgerow trees (Ligustrum, Eucalyptus) and field-margin vegetation in sustaining these populations as potential sunflower pollinators.

This 1908 field note describes a male mating aggregation display ('sun-dance') observed at a Melissodes nesting site in Augusta, Georgia, in which yellow-clypeus males repeatedly chase, dodge, and grapple with black-clypeus females returning to their burrows carrying pollen loads, which Turner interprets as a 'nuptial ambuscade' facilitating copulation. It also notes Nomadidae (cuckoo bees), a cleptoparasitic bee family, loitering near Melissodes burrows waiting to oviposit on the bees' stored pollen provisions.

This is Part I of LaBerge's monographic revision of Melissodes for North and Central America, so far covering the introduction, phylogenetic and geographic-variation discussion, the key to subgenera, the complete subgenus Brachymelissodes (cressonii, minima), and a large part of subgenus Epimelissodes: full species accounts for M. atripes, M. albocollaris, M. grandissima, the newly described M. aegis, M. comanche, M. machaerantherae, M. helianthelli, the newly described M. nitida, an extensive account of M. obliqua with three subspecies (obliqua, expurgata, caliginosa) including a nesting-biology account (Custer, Colorado) describing Triepeolus concavus as a cleptoparasite, M. texana with the new subspecies M. texana eluta, M. petulca with its two subspecies (petulca, suffusa; with illinoensis and townsendi treated as synonyms), including a geographic pie-graph analysis of the Texas intergradation zone between the subspecies and extensive flower records dominated by Compositae (especially Helianthus (sunflower), Ratibida, Gaillardia, Rudbeckia, Coreopsis, and Helenium), and the start of the species account of M. sabinensis (Epimelissodes), a species of three largely allopatric subspecies distinguished from petulca suffusa mainly by male mesepisternal hair density and genitalic characters. THIS RECORD IS PARTIAL — only pages 911-1020 of a roughly 250-page work have been processed so far; topics/keywords/species/overview will be revised as later batches (covering the remaining subgenera and species) are added.

Describes the female of Melissodes ablusus from Millbrae, California (type and seven paratypes, collected 1 September 1912), noting its ferruginous flagellum, variable thoracic hair and creamy-white hairs on the hind basitarsi and tibiae. The author treats it as a slightly modified form of Melissodes metenua from Oregon, and notes that the mouth parts are typical of Melissodes and that the bees had collected light orange pollen, apparently from Asteraceae (composites).

Reports the five Melissodes taken at Waldoboro, southern Maine, including Melissodes desponsus, Melissodes agilis (with a partial gynandromorph male), Melissodes illatus and Melissodes apicatus, giving flight dates, flower records and diagnostic notes. In the Melissodes portion of this publication, Say describes Melissodes bimaculatus bimaculatus (referred to as Macrocera binotata) from Indiana: the female is black with short thoracic hair, blackish violaceous wings, a white spot of prostrate hair on each side of the fourth tergal segment and whitish long hairs on the posterior tibiae and tarsi, while the slightly smaller male has a pale yellow nasus and labrum, paler wings and an immaculate tergum. Say notes some specific similarity to the preceding Macrocera species but, with much hesitation, gives it a distinct place. Say also describes Melissodes druriellus (referred to as Macrocera rustica) from Indiana, with white tergal bands (double on the second segment), whitish thoracic hair, a white male nasus and longer male antennae, and compares it with Peponapis pruinosa (referred to as Macrocera pruinosa).
